## `need.md`: Need for the review

**What the review is about.** Message abstractions (objects and actors that own their state and talk only through messages) are used in languages, agents and networks. The operating system, the instruction set and the hardware underneath still expose threads, shared memory and primitives that are not messages. The review collects the systems that tried to carry message semantics below the language, into the kernel, the instruction set or the hardware. For each it records how far down it got, what non-message primitives it kept, how it performed, and why it was abandoned or not adopted.

**Existing reviews**

| Review | What it covers | Why it is not enough |
|---|---|---|
| Levy (1984). *Capability-Based Computer Systems*. Digital Press. | "An introduction, a survey, a history, and an evaluation of capability- and object-based computer systems" (p. vii): B5000, Plessey 250, CAP, Hydra, StarOS, System/38, Intel 432 (pp. vii–viii). | Its focus is capability addressing and protection, not message passing as the only means of communication (pp. vii–viii). Published in 1984, so it misses the J-Machine (1992), multikernels (2009) and everything after the end of Dennard scaling. It is a narrative survey with no stated selection method. |
| Ditzel, Patterson (1980). *Retrospective on High-Level Language Computer Architecture*. ISCA 7, 97–104. | Survey and critique of architectures built for high-level languages. Taken from Wikipedia's "High-level language computer architecture" article; the full text was not reached. | Covers language-directed machines before 1980, not message-based or actor machines, operating systems, or multicore. Has no stated selection method, but this is unverified because the full text was not read. |
| Li, Zhang, Li, Fong (2012). *Object-Oriented Programming Hardware/Software Supports and Comparison*. ICCIA 2. | Compares three ways to support object-oriented programs: compilation to native code, software virtual machines, and object machines (abstract). | About running objects faster on one processor. Does not cover message passing, actors, operating systems or multiple cores (abstract). Not a systematic review. |
| De Koster, Van Cutsem, De Meuter (2016). *43 Years of Actors: A Taxonomy of Actor Models and Their Key Properties*. AGERE 2016. | History and taxonomy of actor languages and libraries in four families: classic actors, active objects, processes, communicating event loops (p. 1). | Language and library level only. Its stated goal "is not to provide an exhaustive overview of every actor system in existence" (p. 1). Does not cover kernels or hardware. |
| de Boer et al. (2017). *A Survey of Active Object Languages*. ACM Computing Surveys 50(5). | Compares four major actor and active-object languages along chosen dimensions (abstract). | Language level only; no operating system or hardware (abstract). |
| Tong (2025). *Descriptor-Based Object-Aware Memory Systems: A Comprehensive Review*. arXiv 2510.27070v2. | Survey of descriptor-based, object-aware memory systems as a way to bridge the semantic gap at the hardware/software interface (p. 1). | Covers memory objects and descriptors, not messages between objects or actors, and not the operating system (p. 1, Fig. 1 p. 2). |

No systematic (Kitchenham-style) review on message semantics below the language level was found. The agent lists the 12 web searches it ran on 2026-10-06; the last four returned primary papers, project pages or forum posts, not reviews.

## `criteria.md`: Selection criteria

A paper is included if it meets at least one inclusion criterion and no exclusion criterion. Each verdict names the criterion that decided it. There is no date limit. "Message-based" means "meets I1".

| ID | Inclusion |
|---|---|
| I1 | The paper describes, implements, simulates or evaluates a processor, instruction set, microarchitecture, multicomputer node or OS kernel in which sending a message, invoking a method on an object, or delivering a message to an actor is a primitive of that level. That means one of: (a) an instruction of the instruction set; (b) a hardware or microcode mechanism; (c) for a kernel, the stated means by which the kernel and its services, or the kernel's own parts, communicate. Examples of (c) are microkernels, multikernels, and operating systems written in an object or actor language that run without a conventional kernel underneath. The paper must name the mechanism with at least one of: message, message passing, send, mailbox, actor, active message, IPC, method invocation. (SQ1–SQ5) |
| I2 | The paper is a retrospective, evaluation or historical account of at least one architecture its authors describe as directed at a high-level language, object-based, object-oriented or message-driven. It must report measured performance or a stated reason for that performance, adoption, abandonment, or the architecture becoming unnecessary. (SQ5, SQ6) |
| I3 | The paper is an empirical study of concurrency defects in real programs or systems, not only the authors' own examples. It must report counts or proportions split by communication mechanism (shared memory vs message passing), or for message-passing-only systems. (SQ7) |

| ID | Exclusion |
|---|---|
| X1 | Meets none of I1–I3. |
| X2 | Applies to papers included only through I1. Excluded if messages appear only at the application, library, runtime, VM or network-protocol level, on a processor with no message mechanism and a kernel that fails I1(c). Examples: an actor library, the Erlang VM, MPI, a Smalltalk VM hosted on Unix or Windows. Does not apply under I2 or I3. |
| X3 | A cluster or network of separate conventional computers, where the message mechanism lies only in the network interface or interconnect between them. |
| X4 | Hardware stated to serve only a fixed function or domain (neural-network inference, DSP, packet switching, graphics) and not stated to run general programs. |
| X5 | Not one of these types: journal article; conference or workshop paper longer than 2 pages; book or chapter; PhD or master's thesis; technical report from a university, research lab or standards body; ACM, IEEE or USENIX magazine article; manufacturer's reference manual. Patents, slides, posters, abstracts of 2 pages or fewer, blogs, forums, encyclopaedias and brochures are excluded. |
| X6 | Full text not in English. |
| X7 | Full text not obtainable from the publisher, an author or institution page, arXiv, Semantic Scholar, the Internet Archive or the university library. The sources tried are recorded. |
| X8 | Same system and same results as another included paper. The longer one is kept; the other is kept too only if it adds a measurement, design element or stated reason. |
| X9 | Presented as a survey, review, overview or taxonomy, with no measurement of its own and no I2 reason of its own. Its reference list is still used for snowballing. |

## `quality.md`: Quality checklist (yes / partly / no)

| ID | Question |
|---|---|
| Q1 | Is the aim or contribution stated explicitly? yes: in one place; partly: has to be inferred from several places; no: not stated. |
| Q2 | Is the communication mechanism described well enough to reimplement it? The four points are message format, naming or addressing, delivery and ordering guarantees, and what happens when the receiver is busy. yes: all four; partly: 1–3; no: none. For I3 studies, the studied programs' mechanisms count instead. |
| Q3 | Does the evidence come from a working artefact? yes: silicon, FPGA, or a kernel running real programs; partly: simulator or emulator; no: design or argument only. For I3: yes: real bug trackers or commits; partly: benchmark suites; no: examples only. |
| Q4 | Is every performance or defect claim measured against a named baseline? yes: each claim; partly: some; no: none. |
| Q5 | Is the measurement setup reported (workloads and why they were chosen, configuration, number of runs or sample size)? yes: all three; partly: one or two; no: none. |
| Q6 | Is every quantitative claim in the abstract and conclusions backed by a table, figure or passage in the body? yes / partly / no. |
| Q7 | Are attributed causes supported by a measurement that isolates them, such as an ablation or breakdown? yes: every cause; partly: some; no: none, or only asserted. |
| Q8 | Are limitations or threats to validity discussed? yes: in a dedicated section or paragraph; partly: in passing; no: not at all. |
| Q9 | Is the evaluation independent of the system's designers? yes: no author is a designer; partly: some are; no: all are, or nothing is evaluated. |

## `extraction-form.md`: Data extraction form

Fields filled for every included paper (`sls/3-reading/P{n}.md`). Every SQ is served by at least one field. Every field also records the page it comes from.

| Field | What to record | Serves |
|---|---|---|
| Reference | Authors, year, title, venue, pages; P ID; the criteria that included it | SQ1–7 |
| Paper type | Design, implementation, evaluation, retrospective, or empirical defect study | SQ1–7 |
| System | Name, year, builder; status (design only / simulated / FPGA / silicon / running kernel / commercial) | SQ1, 5, 6 |
| Levels with message semantics | For each level (hardware, microcode, ISA, kernel, runtime/VM, language): is a send the primitive? yes / no / not stated | SQ1 |
| Receiving unit and state ownership | What receives messages; whether its state can be read or written by anything else, and how | SQ1, 2, 7 |
| Message mechanism | Synchronous or asynchronous; how the receiver is named; ordering and delivery guarantees; buffering; behaviour when busy; dispatch | SQ1, 3 |
| Non-message primitives | Every non-send mechanism kept (shared or global memory, interrupts, traps, privileged instructions, microcode, global registers, DMA, I/O ports…), and at which level | SQ2 |
| Self-definition | Which levels are written in the system's own objects and messages and which are outside the model; whether a running program can inspect or change them | SQ2 |
| Interposition | Can a third component sit between sender and receiver without changing either? Mechanism and level | SQ3 |
| OS functions | Protection, scheduling, resource allocation, naming, failure handling: how each is provided, and whether a central component is involved | SQ4 |
| Cost of message primitives | Latency or cycles of one send, one dispatch, one context or actor switch, and on what hardware | SQ5 |
| Performance results | Metric, workload, system, baseline (name, version, configuration), value for each, unit | SQ5 |
| Scaling | Core or node counts, metric, result at each count, baseline | SQ5 |
| Attributed causes | Each cause the authors give, quoted or paraphrased closely, and whether a measurement isolates it | SQ5, 6 |
| Fate and reasons | What happened to the system and every reason given for it; who states it (designers or a third party) | SQ6 |
| Concurrency defects | Population, number of defects, categories, counts per mechanism, defects a design claims to prevent by construction | SQ7 |
| Quality | Q1–Q9, each with a page | SQ1–7 |
| Notes | Anything relevant to an SQ that no field above captures | SQ1–7 |

## SQ1–SQ7

Each file holds the question, *Why it matters to the observation*, and *Origin*.

**SQ1** (origin: observation): Which computer systems provide sending a message (to an object, actor, process or core) as a primitive below the programming language, that is in the operating system kernel, the instruction set or the hardware? At which of these levels does each system's message semantics hold?
*Why:* the observation claims message abstractions stop above the OS and the hardware. This tests that claim against the systems that tried to go lower, and maps how far down each one got.

**SQ2** (observation): In the systems found by SQ1, which mechanisms that are not message sends remain (shared memory, interrupts, traps, privileged instructions, microcode, global registers)? Which levels of each system are written in the system's own objects and messages?
*Why:* the observation says systems below the language rest on primitives that break their own rules, so they can't define themselves. This finds where each attempt kept such escape routes and how far its self-definition reached.

**SQ3** (observation): Which message-based systems below the language level let a component (a proxy, monitor, filter or load balancer) be placed between a sender and a receiver without changing either, and by what mechanism?
*Why:* networks allow layers in between because their parts talk only through messages, while low-level machines expose shared state where no layer can be put in between. Did earlier attempts below the language keep that property?

**SQ4** (notes): How do operating systems and machines built from message-passing parts that share no state provide protection, scheduling, resource allocation and naming? Which of these functions still rely on a central coordinator?
*Why:* the notes aim for no central coordinator and leave open how the usual OS functions would be provided.

**SQ5** (notes): What performance have message-based or object-based processors, instruction sets and kernels reported against conventional baselines? This includes the cost of one message send and the scaling with core count, and the causes the authors give for the differences.
*Why:* gathers the measured evidence H2 and H3 rest on, and the baselines and metrics later steps can reuse.

**SQ6** (notes): According to their designers and to later evaluations, why were language-directed, object-based and message-based machines abandoned, not adopted, or made unnecessary?
*Why:* H1 must be checked against the stated reasons for their decline.

**SQ7** (notes): What do empirical studies report about the number and kinds of concurrency defects in programs or systems where each piece of state has one owner and is changed only through messages, compared with programs or systems that share memory?
*Why:* the notes motivate the thesis with shared-state bugs and already name the Go counter-evidence. This collects both sides.

## SQ8–SQ19 (origin: counter-evidence, added by skeptic)

**SQ8:** What empirical evidence shows that the hardware's execution model, rather than the language, libraries, tools or training, determines how programmers design and write programs, and how correct those programs are?
*Why:* the premise "the machine model shapes how programs are written" rests only on two Turing Award lectures, which are essays, not measurements. If the language or runtime decides, changing the hardware doesn't change the programs, and the motivation needs another basis.

**SQ9:** What evidence and arguments show that narrowing the semantic gap, by raising the hardware interface toward the language, harms performance, cost, generality or compiler optimisation? Do those arguments apply to a message send as the machine's primitive?
*Why:* the RISC argument (Patterson & Ditzel 1980) was made against exactly this goal. If it carries over, the observation describes a deliberate trade-off, not an oversight.

**SQ10:** What does the literature report about the equivalence (duality) of message-passing and shared-memory system structures? Can either be built on the other while keeping its properties (encapsulation, freedom from data races, interposition) and its performance?
*Why:* Lauer & Needham (1978/79) argue the two are duals. If so, the gap may only be about which layer exposes which model, and putting messages in hardware may add nothing a layer above can't give.

**SQ11:** Why do developers of actor or message-passing programs also use shared state, locks or other concurrency mechanisms alongside messages? What do they report that the pure message model can't express or makes too costly?
*Why:* Tasharofi, Dinges & Johnson (2013, ECOOP) report that most large actor programs they studied mix models, partly because of shortcomings of the actor model itself. If programmers build escape routes whenever they can, a machine that removes them may be unusable rather than cleaner.

**SQ12:** Where do measured costs and scaling limits come from in actor and message-passing runtimes on conventional hardware? Do their authors name the hardware's shared-memory model as the limiting factor, or report software techniques that remove the limit?
*Why:* compiler techniques already made language-specific processors unnecessary for Smalltalk and Self. If actor runtimes (e.g. on the Savina benchmarks, Imam & Sarkar 2014) hit limits a message machine wouldn't change, the "improve execution" half of the design problem is lost.

**SQ13:** Which many-core processors were built without hardware shared memory or cache coherence, communicating between cores by messages or channels? How were they programmed, and why were they discontinued or not adopted?
*Why:* H3's target has been built before: the Transputer with occam channels, and Intel's 48-core SCC (Howard et al. 2010, ISSCC). If those were dropped for reasons that still apply, H3 doesn't separate this work from earlier failures.

**SQ14:** What evidence shows that hardware shared memory, cache coherence and shared-memory OS kernels scale to many cores? What limits do studies report on many-core scaling in general (power, communication, serial fractions)?
*Why:* three sources each weaken a premise of H3 or of the parallel-hardware motivation:
- Martin, Hill & Sorin (2012, CACM): coherence can scale.
- Boyd-Wickizer et al. (2010, OSDI): no scalability reason to give up traditional kernels on 48 cores.
- Esmaeilzadeh et al. (2011, ISCA): dark silicon limits multicore scaling.

**SQ15:** Which system functions (resource allocation, scheduling, naming, protection, failure handling, global consistency) have been shown to require global agreement, or to work better with central or logically central coordination? What do decentralised versions cost or give up?
*Why:* agreement among message-passing parts has proven limits (FLP 1985), and networking, the notes' own model, moved toward logically central control with SDN (Kreutz et al. 2015). If key OS functions need a coordinator, "no central coordinator" may make RQ5's answer "no" by construction.

**SQ16:** What do studies of reflective and metacircular systems report about whether a system can be defined entirely in its own terms? What must remain outside it as a base, and what does that base cost or prevent?
*Why:* Smith's reflective tower (1984, POPL) is an infinite stack of levels, at least virtually, and Squeak's VM is written in Smalltalk but translated to C to run (Ingalls et al. 1997). If every self-defining system needs an outside base, the goal becomes moving the base, not removing it.

**SQ17:** Which mechanisms let a layer be put between a program and conventional shared-memory hardware or kernels without changing either (virtual memory, trap-and-emulate virtualisation, system call interposition, IOMMU)? How do their coverage and cost compare with interposition on messages?
*Why:* the observation says low-level layers "cannot be put in between the way the network allows", yet virtualisation does exactly that (Popek & Goldberg 1974). SQ3 only looks at message-based systems, so it can't find this.

**SQ18:** What costs of object-based and capability-based hardware do independent evaluations attribute to object orientation, fine-grained protection or object addressing themselves, rather than to compilers or implementation? How large are those costs?
*Why:* H2 rests on one paper by the 432's own evaluators, and that paper still names a 1–4× residual slowdown as inherent (Colwell et al. 1988, pp. 336–337, via the notes). Hansen et al. 1982 (citation not fully verified) and CHERI (Woodruff et al. 2014, ISCA) measure the cost from other angles.

**SQ19:** Since the end of Dennard scaling, which kinds of specialised architectures have been adopted and which have failed? What factors (software compatibility, ecosystem, programmability, economics, kind of workload) do analyses give for the difference?
*Why:* the specialisation that succeeded may be narrow and data-parallel (the TPU, Jouppi et al. 2018), far from general-purpose actor machines. The barriers that sank earlier machines may not have changed.

# Agent contract

What every agent in `.claude/agents/` does, whatever its role. The agent's own file adds only its role.

## You receive
From the step skill that dispatched you:
- **Row:** the flow row you run (e.g. `3a`), defined in `ai/flow-sls.md` or `ai/flow-dsrm.md`.
- **Inputs:** the exact files you read. Paths are relative to `research/` unless they start with `ai/` or `artifact/`.
- **Outputs:** the exact files you write.

## You do
1. Read the row in its flow file, then every input file. Read nothing else from `research/`; your view of the research is the inputs.
2. For each output, copy its template from `ai/template/` (the table in `ai/template/README.md` maps output to template) and fill every `{placeholder}`.
3. Set the frontmatter: `id`, `row`, `by:` your agent name, `status: proposed`, `inputs:` the files you read.
4. Write only the output files. Every other file, and every `status`, belongs to me.

## Your output is done when
- Every output file exists and has every section of its template.
- No `{placeholder}` or `[ ]` is left. A field you cannot fill says why, in one line.
- Every claim about a paper carries its P ID and page, or the reference and page for papers not yet in the review.
- Every fact comes from a file or source you actually read in this run. A fact you cannot trace to one is left out and named in your report.

## You return
A short report to the skill:
- Each file written, with one line on what it holds.
- Open issues: fields you could not fill, sources you could not reach, decisions you found that are mine to make.

The last file, **`extraction-form.md`**, must have at least one field for every SQ you kept (`step.md`). Right now it only covers SQ1–SQ7. Here are the proposed edits:

**Edits to existing fields, matching the SQ changes and the skeptic's fixes:**
1. *Levels with message semantics* (SQ1): "yes" means every state change at that level is caused by a message send, with no other path. Also record whether the system started message-based at a level and later added non-message paths.
2. *Non-message primitives* (SQ2): add the reason the paper gives for keeping each.
3. *Self-definition* (SQ2, **SQ16**): add what stays outside as a base, and what that base costs or prevents.
4. *Interposition* (SQ3, **SQ17**): also covers conventional hardware and kernels (virtual memory, virtualisation, system call interposition, IOMMU). Add the cost.
5. *OS functions* (SQ4, **SQ15**): replicated parts that must agree count as coordination. Add what each decentralised version costs or gives up.
6. *Attributed causes* (SQ5, **SQ18**): add who states each cause (designers or a third party), and whether it's inherent to the design or due to its implementation.
7. *Concurrency defects* (SQ7): record every defect kind, including deadlocks, message-protocol violations and message-order defects.

**New fields:**

| Field | What to record | Serves |
|---|---|---|
| What shapes programs | What the paper finds determines how programs are designed and how correct they are (hardware model, language, libraries, tools, training), and the kind of evidence | SQ8 |
| Hardware–language trade-off | Each argued or measured cost or benefit of raising the hardware interface toward the language or of specialising it (performance, cost, generality, compiler optimisation), and whether it applies to a message send as the primitive | SQ9 |
| Model equivalence | Which model is built on which (messages on shared memory or the reverse); which properties (encapsulation, freedom from data races, interposition) and how much performance are kept or lost | SQ10 |
| Model mixing | Non-message mechanisms used in actor or message programs, how often, and the reasons developers give | SQ11 |
| Runtime limits | Where actor or message runtimes' costs and scaling limits come from; whether the hardware's shared-memory model is named as the cause, or a software technique removes it | SQ12 |
| Many-core scaling | Core counts; whether there is shared memory or coherence; how inter-core communication works; the scaling result; the limits named (power, communication, serial fraction) | SQ13, SQ14 |
| Adoption factors | For each specialised architecture: adopted or not, and the factors the paper gives (software compatibility, ecosystem, programmability, economics, kind of workload) | SQ6, SQ13, SQ19 |

**Also:** *Reference*, *Paper type*, *Quality* and *Notes* will serve SQ1–SQ19 instead of SQ1–SQ7.

# Protocol change: i3-shared-memory-baseline

Saved as `sls/1-protocol/changes/2026-10-06-i3-shared-memory-baseline.md`.

## What changed
`criteria.md`, I3. Before: "…either split by communication mechanism (shared memory versus message passing) or for programs or systems built on message passing only. (SQ7)". After: "…either split by communication mechanism (shared memory versus message passing) or for programs or systems built on message passing only, or for programs or systems built on shared memory only, as the comparison baseline for SQ7. (SQ7)".

## Why
SQ7 asks for the comparison with programs or systems that share memory, but I3 as written let in no shared-memory-only defect study, so SQ7 had no shared-memory side. Found at gate 2b: the seed Lu et al. (2008), R0-005, failed I3 as written.

## Papers affected
None have P IDs yet (gate 2b not done). In `sls/2-search/R0.md`, R0-005 and the bug-study candidates (search block B3) are re-screened against the new I3 in the 2a rerun.
""")

content.text:
P12 (the Message-Driven Processor) is now read, so 3 of the 8 pilot papers are done. The other 5 readers are still running, and citation checks are running on all three records.

The reader could only get the authors' 25-page preprint, not the published IEEE Micro version, so the record cites preprint pages. The preprint has no figures. On substance, no level of the processor is fully message-based. Task creation is message-only, but:
- the instruction set extends a conventional processor's;
- the compiler turns message sends into direct calls when the type is known;
- the run-time kernel is entered with an ordinary procedure call.

This adds two choices for the 3c gate:
- **IEEE Micro version:** you could get it through the library so the record cites the version of record.
- **Format fixes:** three more extraction-form changes.
  - Allow a second paper type.
  - Record which operations at a level are message-only.
  - Mark each cost figure as measured, simulated or a design figure.

content.text:
P22 (Martin, Hill & Sorin, *Why On-Chip Cache Coherence Is Here to Stay*) is read: 4 of 8 pilot papers done. Its citation check is running, along with those for P5, P9 and P12. Readers for P8, P10, P13 and P33 are still working.

Like P12, the record cites the authors' near-final manuscript, not the published CACM version, because the ACM site refused the download.

Findings that bear on SQ14:
- **The claim:** coherence traffic per cache miss doesn't grow with core count when the sharers are tracked exactly. The storage overhead is about 2% at 512 cores with a three-level cache hierarchy.
- **The evidence:** almost all of it is analysis. The only thing actually run is one simulation on a synthetic workload.
- **Independence:** the authors evaluate their own design, so Q9 is "no". One author discloses a financial interest in AMD.

The pattern across readers is now clear:
- **Fields that don't apply:** all four readers asked for an "Applies to" column in the extraction form.
- **Pages and source version:** three asked for a rule on which pages to cite when only a preprint or manuscript is available. P5 and P9 also disagree on proceedings pages versus PDF pages.

New for the 3c gate:
- **Paper type:** add a "position or analytical argument" type.
- **Analytical models:** say how Q3 and Q4 score them.

content.text:
P8 (the Multikernel) is read in full: 5 of 8 pilot papers done. Its citation check is running alongside those for P5, P9, P12 and P22. Readers for P10, P13 and P33 are still working.

The P8 reader found two more things the form can't express:
- **Levels with message semantics:** a multikernel is message-based *between* cores but not *within* one, where traps, interrupts and system calls go into each core's driver. The field allows only one yes/no per level, so the reader suggests asking about the two separately.
- **OS functions:** the rule "replicated parts that must agree count as coordination" marks protection and memory as coordinated, even though the system has no single central component. That hides a distinction your SQ4 cares about.

The P8 reader also agrees with the others:
- **Paper type** should allow several values.
- Fields that don't apply should be marked `n/a: reason`.
- A rule is needed for which pages to cite when the copy read isn't the publisher's.

I'm still holding everything for one set of choices at the 3c gate, once the last three readers and all eight citation checks are back.

    - **Source:** the published ACM TOCS version, pp. 296–339. It is a CiteSeerX scan with OCR, taken from the Internet Archive item `432_complexity_paper`.
    - **Pages:** journal page = PDF page + 295.

    - The ACM DL PDF, which OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar list as bronze open access, returned HTTP 403.
    - Its only Wayback Machine capture with a 200 status redirected to a 403 capture and could not be loaded.
    - The Princeton course copy returned 404.
    - The Internet Archive copy worked on retry.
  - **Quality scores:** Q1 yes, Q2 partly, Q3 partly (mostly simulator), Q4 partly, Q5 partly, Q6 partly, Q7 partly, Q8 yes, Q9 yes.
    - For Q9, I checked that none of the three authors wrote the 432 design papers the paper cites.

    - The text says the CFA benchmarks improve by 30–40 % (p. 329), but Table XVI shows 39.6–44.7 %.
    - Table XXI repeats 4,489,605 for Sieve as both cycles saved and remaining cycles (p. 336).
    - The "inherent cost" ratio appears as 2–3x (p. 336), 3–4x (p. 336), 1–4x slower (p. 337) and "one-fourth to one times the speed" (p. 296).
    - So synthesis will need to cite more than one value.

Send latency, ordering and what happens when the receiver is busy are left to Cox et al. 1983, ACM TOCS 1(1) (ref. [6], p. 338). That paper, Gehringer and Colwell 1986 (ISCA), and Colwell's 1985 CMU thesis CMU-CS-85-159 are good snowballing targets.
  - **Concept IDs:** I had no C files among my inputs, so every concept is marked "new". They need reconciling at 4a.
  - **Inputs:** besides the listed inputs, I also read `research/papers/README.md` to learn how PDFs are published.

  9. **System, "year built":** only "conceived 1975" is given.
  10. **Quality:**
      - Q3: "partly" for simulator evidence with only light silicon corroboration is debatable.
      - Q5: for a deterministic cycle-level simulator, "number of runs" means little.
      - Q6: it is unclear whether ranges that disagree count as "reported".
  
  ### Decisions that are yours
  **D1. Criterion for R0-010.** The paper describes an instruction set with a Send instruction it calls "an interprocess communication primitive" (p. 298), which looks like I1(a).

  - (b) Record I1 as well: in `research/sls/2-search/R0.md` row R0-010, change the verdict column `include | I2` to `include | I1, I2` and add "Send instruction, I1(a), p. 298" to the reason. Also change the Reference line in `P10.md` to "included under I1 and I2".
  - **I recommend (b).** The paper meets I1(a) on its own text, and recording it makes the paper count for SQ1–SQ3 evidence.
  
  **D2. Publishing P10.pdf in the public `papers` release.** It is an ACM-copyrighted scan, not the publisher's own file. The notice on p. 296 allows copying that is not for direct commercial advantage, as long as the ACM notice stays on the copy.
  - (a) Publish as usual with `just papers-push`: no file edit.
  - (b) Keep it local only: delete `research/papers/P10.pdf` before pushing, or add an exclusion for it, and add a line to the Notes in `P10.md` pointing to the DOI and the Internet Archive item.
  - **I recommend (a).** The release is non-commercial and the scan keeps the ACM notice, which is the condition the notice sets.
  
  **D3. Which "inherent cost" figure synthesis should use.**
  - (a) Use the authors' explicit estimate, 2–3x (p. 336).
  - (b) Use the conclusion's 1–4x (p. 337).
  - (c) Cite both, with pages, and note the disagreement.
  - **I recommend (c).** No record edit is needed now; it applies at 4a.
  
</agent-message>

The pilot is done: 8 records and 7 citation checks (P13 is waiting on its full text). Opening the **3c gate (records accepted)**.

**What the pilot showed**
- **Accuracy:** about 92–97% of cited claims check out in every record, and no numbers were invented.
- **One problem repeats:** every reader *strengthens* the paper. It drops hedges ("usually", "may"), turns inferences into page-cited facts, or cites the wrong page.
- **The citation check works:** it caught all of these, and every checker proposed exact one-line fixes.

I'll ask in order: the records first, then the reading rules for the remaining 272 papers, then PDF publishing. Each checker's exact edits are listed in `research/sls/3-reading/P{n}.citations.md`, under its decision section.

options.label: Between vs within cores

lines: | Interposition | Not stated as interposition. Related mechanisms: all transports sit behind a common interface (p. 10), the protocol and transport are late-bound (p. 6), and the name service maps a name to a service reference (p. 10). These suggest a transport or service could be swapped without changing the sender or receiver, but the paper neither claims nor measures this. | pp. 6, 10 |

| Operating system functions | *Protection*: each core's CPU driver enforces protection and authorisation (p. 8), and capabilities are modelled on seL4 (p. 10). Coordination is involved: yes, because all cores must keep their capability lists consistent (p. 10). *Scheduling*: the CPU driver time-slices locally and runs dispatchers by upcalls, with user-level thread schedulers (pp. 8–9). Cross-core threads are handled by messages, and CPU drivers can be coordinated for gang scheduling (p. 11). Central component: not stated. *Memory*: virtual memory is managed at user level through capabilities (p. 10). Unmap uses a one-phase commit and retype a two-phase commit between all monitors (p. 11). That is coordination: yes. *Devices*: drivers are user-level processes (p. 8), placed on cores by the system knowledge base (p. 11). Whether the SKB is one instance: not stated. *Naming*: a name service (p. 10); centralisation not stated. *Failure*: none; "the complete system is a failure unit" (p. 17). *Costs of decentralising*: the capability scheme "was a mistake … unnecessarily complex, and no more efficient than scalable per-processor memory managers" (p. 10). Replica consistency adds latency and developer burden (p. 7). Two-phase commit "serializes more messages" than shootdown (p. 14). | pp. 7–11, 14, 17 |

| Cost of message primitives | Same-core LRPC, one way (Table 1): 845 cycles on 2×4 Intel, 757 on 2×2 AMD, 1463 on 4×4 AMD, 1549 on 8×4 AMD (p. 9). L4 raw IPC is about 420 cycles on 2×2 AMD (p. 8). Inter-core URPC latency (Table 2): 180 cycles (shared cache) to 618 cycles (two hops, 8×4 AMD) (p. 10). URPC against L4 IPC on 2×2 AMD (Table 3): 450 vs 424 cycles; 3.42 vs 2.36 messages per kcycle; 9 vs 25 I-cache lines; 8 vs 13 D-cache lines (p. 10). IPI wake cost C ≈ 6000 cycles (p. 14). A trap costs ≈ 800 cycles (p. 12). | pp. 8–10, 12, 14 |

-| Performance results | (a) Update shared state, 4×4 AMD: SHM costs ~12,000 extra cycles per update at 16 cores, against under 30 on one core. MSG beats SHM for 4 or more cache lines (Fig. 3, pp. 3–4). (b) URPC pipelined throughput: 2.75–11.97 messages per kcycle (Table 2, p. 10). (c) Unmap latency, 8×4 AMD, Barrelfish vs Linux 2.6.26 mprotect vs Windows Server 2008 R2 Beta VirtualProtect: at 32 cores, about 18k vs 29k vs 45k cycles, read off Fig. 7. Barrelfish is slower at 2 cores (≈10k vs ≈5–6k) (p. 13). (d) Two-phase commit, 8×4 AMD: ≈14k to ≈28k cycles single-operation and ≈8k to ≈19k pipelined, 2 to 32 cores, read off Fig. 8 (p. 14). (e) IP loopback, 2×2 AMD, Barrelfish vs Linux (version not stated): 2154 vs 1823 Mbit/s; 21 vs 77 D-cache misses per packet; HyperTransport link utilisation 8%/3% vs 11%/9% (Table 4, p. 14). (f) OpenMP (CG, FT, IS) and SPLASH-2 (Barnes-Hut, radiosity), 4×4 AMD, Barrelfish vs Linux with GCC 4.3.3 and GOMP: similar on FT, Barnes-Hut and radiosity. Barrelfish is better on CG at 11–16 cores (worse at 7–9 cores) and worse on IS (Fig. 9, p. 15). (g) UDP echo, 2×4 Intel, e1000: 951.7 vs 951 Mbit/s for Linux 2.6.26 (p. 16). (h) Static web page, 2×2 AMD: 18697 req/s (640 Mbit/s) vs 8924 req/s (316 Mbit/s) for lighttpd 1.4.23 on Linux 2.6.26 (tuned). Web-plus-SQLite: 3417 req/s, with no baseline (p. 16). | pp. 3–4, 10, 13–16 |

+| Performance results | (a) Update shared state, 4×4 AMD: SHM costs ~12,000 extra cycles per update at 16 cores, against under 30 on one core. MSG beats SHM for 4 or more cache lines (Fig. 3, pp. 3–4). (b) URPC pipelined throughput: 2.75–11.97 messages per kcycle (Table 2, p. 10). (c) Unmap latency, 8×4 AMD, Barrelfish vs Linux 2.6.26 mprotect vs Windows Server 2008 R2 Beta VirtualProtect: at 32 cores, about 18k vs 29k vs 45k cycles, read off Fig. 7. Barrelfish is slower at 2 cores (≈10k vs ≈5–6k) (p. 13). (d) Two-phase commit, 8×4 AMD: ≈14k to ≈28k cycles single-operation and ≈8k to ≈19k pipelined, 2 to 32 cores, read off Fig. 8 (p. 14). (e) IP loopback, 2×2 AMD, Barrelfish vs Linux (version not stated): 2154 vs 1823 Mbit/s; 21 vs 77 D-cache misses per packet; HyperTransport link utilisation 8%/3% vs 11%/9% (Table 4, p. 14). (f) OpenMP (CG, FT, IS) and SPLASH-2 (Barnes-Hut, radiosity), 4×4 AMD, Barrelfish vs Linux with GCC 4.3.3 and GOMP: similar on FT, Barnes-Hut and radiosity. Barrelfish is better on CG at 11–16 cores (worse at 7–9, read off) and worse on IS (Fig. 9, p. 15). (g) UDP echo, 2×4 Intel, e1000: 951.7 vs 951 Mbit/s for Linux 2.6.26 (p. 16). (h) Static web page, 2×2 AMD: 18697 req/s (640 Mbit/s) vs 8924 req/s (316 Mbit/s) for lighttpd 1.4.23 on Linux 2.6.26 (tuned). Web-plus-SQLite: 3417 req/s, with no baseline (p. 16). | pp. 3–4, 10, 13–16 |

| Scaling | Fig. 3: 2–16 cores, against shared-memory updates (p. 3). Figs. 6–8: 2–32 cores on 8×4 AMD. NUMA-aware multicast is near flat at ≈3k cycles; broadcast and unicast grow linearly to ≈13–14k (Fig. 6, read off the plot). For unmap and two-phase commit see *Performance results* (pp. 13–14). Fig. 9: 1–16 cores against Linux (p. 15). The authors: "It would be wrong to draw any quantitative conclusions from our large-scale benchmarks" (p. 16). | pp. 3, 13–16 |

| Attributed causes | All are stated by the designers. (1) SHM cost: "All of these extra cycles are spent with the core stalled on cache misses". Inherent to coherent shared memory; not isolated beyond the SHM/MSG contrast (p. 3). (2) Broadcast shootdown is slow "due to the cache-coherence protocol used by AMD64": the line crosses the interconnect N times. Hardware cause; explained, not separately measured (p. 12). (3) The flat unicast curve below 8 cores is "likely" the stride prefetcher. Speculation (p. 13). (4) Multicast wins because the shared L3 removes interconnect traffic and eight processors send in parallel. Design; shown by the protocol comparison in Fig. 6 (p. 13). (5) Unmap overhead above the base protocol is "largely due to inefficiencies in the message dispatch loop of the user-level threads package". Implementation; not isolated (p. 13). (6) Linux and Windows unmap scale worse because of "serially sending IPIs" (p. 13). Not isolated. (7) Loopback gain: URPC avoids shared memory except the channel and payload, while "Linux causes more cache-coherence traffic"; also kernel crossings. Design; partly isolated by the miss and HyperTransport counters (p. 14). (8) Fig. 9 differences come from "our user-space threads library vs. the Linux in-kernel implementation". Implementation; not isolated (p. 15). (9) Web server gain is "mainly due to avoiding kernel-user crossings". Design; not isolated (p. 16). (10) The CPU-driver/monitor split costs several thousand cycles per OS call. Implementation choice; not measured in a figure (p. 12). | pp. 3, 12–16 |

| Fate and reasons | The paper reports a research prototype, "not by any means yet a mature system" (p. 17). Its source is released (p. 18), and an ARM port to programmable NICs is in progress (p. 17). It states no later fate. | pp. 17–18 |

- **Quality:** answer each Q from the paper's text, with a one-line reason.
- **Concepts:** name the paper's concepts in its own terms; reuse an existing C ID only when the meaning matches its definition.

+- **Faithful to the paper:** keep the paper's own hedges (usually, may, suggest) and scope (which benchmark, which machine, which configuration). Anything the paper does not state, mark `(inferred)`. Values estimated from a plot, mark `(read off)`. Quote, don't paraphrase, any claim a field turns on. The ACM DL PDF (dl.acm.org) returned 403. This copy is a facsimile reprint. Its first page carries the original ACM line "© 1992 ACM 0-89791-509-7/92/0005/0256" (original first page 256), but it is numbered 430–440, consistent with the 1998 *25 Years of ISCA* selected-papers reprint. That identification is inferred from the numbering and creation date, not stated in the file. **All pages in this record are the printed reprint pages 430–440.** Original ISCA '92 page = reprint page − 174 (430 → 256), inferred from the first-page ACM line.

- **Early-stop path:** I read the abstract and introduction first (p. 430–431). They did not clearly trigger X3: the abstract promises "a range of enhancements to mainstream processors" (p. 430), and §1.3 announces a study of message-driven architectures, where "message send is supported directly in the execution unit" (p. 431). -- **Verdict after full text (proposed; yours to decide):**
+- **Verdict after full text (decided at gate 3c, 2026-10-06: include under I2, I1(b) partly):**

- X3 is partly true of the paper's own implementations. The nCUBE/2 and CM-5 are distributed-memory multicomputers whose kernels fail I1(c), and the Active Message layer sits on their network interfaces (p. 431–433).

- X3 does not fit the paper as a whole. §3 analyses the J-Machine and Monsoon, where message send and reception are processor mechanisms (SEND instruction, hardware scheduling queue; p. 436, p. 438). §4 proposes processor mechanisms for message handlers: PC injection, user-level interrupts, message registers, a dual message processor (p. 438–439).

- The paper also meets I2. It evaluates architectures it calls "message driven" and states a reason for their processing performance (lack of locality; p. 435–437, p. 440). I2 exempts the paper from X2. X3 has no I2 exemption in criteria.md, but its condition is not met by the message-driven machines.

# Protocol change: reading-pilot

Saved as \`sls/1-protocol/changes/2026-10-06-reading-pilot.md\`.

## What changed
- \`extraction-form.md\`:
  - New *Applies to* column (I1–I4 per field); a field outside the paper's criteria is \`n/a (I3)\`, and \`not stated\` means the field applies but the paper is silent.
  - Values in *Cost of message primitives*, *Performance results* and *Scaling* are tagged measured / simulated / design figure / analytical / read off.
  - *Reference*: pages are those printed on \`papers/P*.pdf\` (else its PDF page), with the version (publisher, preprint, manuscript, reprint), the publisher's page range and any offset; abstract-only content cites \`abstract\`. Criteria I1–I4.
  - *Paper type*: one or more types, plus "position or analytical argument".
  - *Levels with message semantics*: adds \`partly\` (a message is a primitive at the level but other paths exist, naming the message-only operations), and for kernels and multicomputers separate answers between cores or nodes and within a core.
- \`quality.md\`:
  - Scale adds \`n/a\`, only for a source not read or a question that cannot apply, with the reason.
  - Q3: analytical models count as no.
  - Q4: a hypothetical baseline counts as partly. For I3, yes if the counts are compared with another named study.
  - Q5: for I3, the sampling procedure replaces the hardware setup.
  - Q9: for I3, yes if no author developed the studied programs.
- \`criteria.md\`, I3: adds "Programs whose defects are reported as accesses to shared variables count as shared-memory programs even if the paper does not use that term."

## Why
The reading pilot (P5, P8, P9, P10, P12, P13, P22, P33) showed the form and the checklist did not fit most papers:
- most fields did not apply to bug studies or analytical papers;
- readers cited five different kinds of page numbers;
- the strict yes/no on levels hid the differences the review is about;
- abstract-only and I3 records could only answer "no" to quality questions that could not apply.

Lu et al. (2008) met I3 only by inference, because it speaks of shared variables, not shared memory.

## Papers affected
The pilot records P5, P8, P9, P10, P12, P13, P22 and P33 were written under the previous form and are not re-read. Their fields are mapped to the new form at synthesis (4a). P5 meets I3 as changed. Every later record uses the new form.
EOF

content.text:
The pilot's 3c gate is applied, the 7 PDFs are published, and `just check` passes. Four records are still waiting on you.

**Record status**
- **Decided:** P5, P22 and P33 are `changed`, with the checker fixes applied. P33 is now included under I2 (`R0-046` updated). P13 is accepted as abstract-only, with a note saying so. Their citation checks are accepted.
- **Waiting on you:** P8, P9, P10 and P12 have their fixes applied but stay `proposed` until you've read them in full, as the reading skill requires for papers your argument depends on. `R0-010` now records I1 alongside I2 for P10, per your choice.
- **The PDFs:** all 7 are in the `papers` release of the public repo: https://github.com/GarroteSantiago/Thesis/releases/tag/papers

**Changes for the remaining 272 papers**
- **Protocol change** `2026-10-06-reading-pilot.md`: the extraction form gets an *Applies to* column with `n/a`, value tags, the page rule, several paper types and `partly` levels. `quality.md` gets the `n/a` value and the readings for bug studies and analytical papers. I3 now counts shared-variable bug studies as shared memory. The 8 pilot records keep the old form; their fields get mapped to the new one at synthesis (4a).
- **Reader rule:** readers must keep the paper's hedges, mark inferences `(inferred)` and plot values `(read off)`, and report any change of inclusion criterion to you.
- **Row 3a inputs:** readers will get the concept files once synthesis creates them.

**One gap I found while applying the fixes.** The citation checkers put their exact fixes in their reports to me, not in the `P{n}.citations.md` files. So the readers couldn't find "option A", and for four records I had to pass the wording on by hand. I'd add a *Suggested fixes* section to the citations template so the fixes live in the file the gate points to. Want me to?

**Next:** once you've read P8, P9, P10 and P12, tell me your decision on each. The plan was batches of about 20 next, starting with the I1 and I2 core papers.

## What's next

3. **Row 4a, synthesis:** the synthesizer builds the concepts from the accepted records. Then the 4b gate, where you decide on them.
4. **Snowballing round 1 (rows 2c and 2d):** backward and forward from P1–P280, then reading and synthesis again. This repeats until a round includes no new papers.
5. **SLS 5:** the gap, the answers to SQ1–SQ19, and the skeptic's attack on the gap. Then the DSRM starts.

Steps 1 and 2 don't depend on your reading of the four key papers, so I can start batch 1 while you read.

content.text:
You can run the full batch; nothing in the workflow forbids it. I'd still do one batch first, for three reasons:

1. **The new rules haven't run on a single paper yet.** The form, the quality scale and the faithfulness rule all changed after the pilot. If something in them is wrong, a full batch means about 270 records to redo; a batch of 20 means 20.
2. **Cost.** In the pilot, one paper took about 120–200k tokens (reader plus checker). For 272 papers that's roughly **35–50 million tokens** and about 540 agent runs. Spending that is easier once the rules are known to work.
3. **Your gate.** All 272 at once means a single 3c gate with 272 records, each with its own fixes and criterion questions. Batches keep each gate to a size you can actually judge. The grouped "accept these" questions help, but not at that scale.

In the full batch's favour: one gate instead of many, and the SLS finishes sooner. Batches don't save any reading; they only change when problems show up.

**My suggestion:** run batch 1 (about 20 core I1/I2 papers) now. If its citation checks come back clean under the new rules, run the remaining ~250 in parallel waves of about 30, with one grouped gate per wave.

Should I start batch 1, or go straight to the full set?
